sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: Medieval European medicine classed ginger as hot and dry and used it to correct conditions thought cold and wet. That reasoning came from [humoral theory](#term:humoral-theory), not from observed outcomes [\[22\]](#cite:22).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: A historical recipe records what people did and why they said they did it. It is evidence about practice, and it is not evidence that the practice worked.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: [Gingerols](#term:gingerol) are the pungent phenolic compounds of fresh ginger. They are thermally unstable and convert to [shogaols](#term:shogaol), which are found in dried ginger and were not detected in fresh [rhizome](#term:rhizome) extracted at ambient temperature [\[3\]](#cite:3).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: A recipe or a trial that used dried ginger involved a chemically different material from one that used fresh, and hot-air drying shifts the balance further toward shogaols as temperature rises [\[4\]](#cite:4).

summary_md: [Gingerols](#term:gingerol) are the pungent phenolic compounds of fresh ginger. They are thermally unstable and convert to [shogaols](#term:shogaol), which are found in dried ginger and were not detected in fresh [rhizome](#term:rhizome) extracted at ambient temperature [\[3\]](#cite:3).

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: In laboratory preparations, ginger extracts and their pungent constituents inhibit the [5-HT3 receptor](#term:5-ht3), the target of standard anti-nausea drugs, and activate [TRPV1](#term:trpv1), the receptor behind pungency [\[56, 61\]](#cite:56,61).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: After people swallow ginger, the free compounds are not detected in plasma; they appear as [conjugates](#term:glucuronide) and are cleared within hours [\[7\]](#cite:7). An explanation built on the free compound has to say where and in what form it acts.

summary_md: In laboratory preparations, ginger extracts and their pungent constituents inhibit the [5-HT3 receptor](#term:5-ht3), the target of standard anti-nausea drugs, and activate [TRPV1](#term:trpv1), the receptor behind pungency [\[56, 61\]](#cite:56,61).
why_here_md: Section 11 sets laboratory mechanisms against human pharmacokinetics.

title: Reading the trials
one_liner: What a meta-analysis, a GRADE rating and a confidence interval do and do not tell you.
why_here: Sections 8 to 10 report pooled estimates and certainty ratings throughout.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect and safety of ginger in the

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md:
A [meta-analysis](#term:meta-analysis) combines trials; an [umbrella review](#term:umbrella-review) combines meta-analyses. The same trials can sit under several reviews, so many reviews do not mean many independent experiments: seven meta-analyses of pregnancy nausea shared 49% of their studies [\[33\]](#cite:33).

[GRADE](#term:grade) rates how far a pooled result can be trusted. For ginger the ratings run from high, for nausea in pregnancy, to very low, for several metabolic outcomes [\[5\]](#cite:5).

A wide [confidence interval](#term:confidence-interval) means the data cannot distinguish no effect from a large one, as with miscarriage risk in the pregnancy trials [\[6\]](#cite:6).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: Sections 8 to 10 give each pooled result with its certainty rating where one exists, and say when an interval is too wide to support a conclusion. <!-- framing -->

title: The ginger plant
one_liner: A sterile, clonally grown member of a large tropical family.
why_here: Sections 2, 4 and 12 assume the reader knows what a rhizome and a cultigen are.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: Ginger is grown from pieces of its [rhizome](#term:rhizome), an underground stem, and is described as a [sterile cultigen](#term:cultigen): it is not known to set seed in cultivation and has no known wild population [\[3, 18\]](#cite:3,18).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: Because every ginger plant is a cutting of an earlier one, its origin cannot be read from wild relatives, and questions about its history turn to documents and, since 2021, to its genome [\[2\]](#cite:2).

summary_md: Ginger is grown from pieces of its [rhizome](#term:rhizome), an underground stem, and is described as a [sterile cultigen](#term:cultigen): it is not known to set seed in cultivation and has no known wild population [\[3, 18\]](#cite:3,18).
why_here_md: Sections 2, 4 and 12 assume the reader knows what a [rhizome](#term:rhizome) and a [cultigen](#term:cultigen) are.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.md: Ginger's compounds inhibit fungi and bacteria in laboratory tests, and infected ginger releases root exudates that suppress bacterial wilt [\[8, 9\]](#cite:8,9).

sections.heading: How this guide uses it
sections.md: Showing that a compound defends a plant requires testing it in the living plant against the organisms that attack it. The sources read for this review do not report that test for [gingerols](#term:gingerol).
